title: Show me I'm wrong
hook: if anyone can show me I'm wrong, I'll gladly change; truth never harmed anyone (Meditations 6.21)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was gymnasium, where a bump in training isn't a plot. Your line was just a scratch.

The last argument you lost. Not on points: lost because the other person was right, and part of you knew it halfway through. What happened next? Often the mind goes hunting for a technicality, a side issue, a tone to object to. Anything but the plain sentence: you're right, I was wrong. Marcus Aurelius spent his days among courtiers and petitioners, and in book six he wrote himself a note that goes the other way. It's an emperor's note, and it opens a door.
screen: `THE ARGUMENT YOU LOST.` → `HUNTING FOR A TECHNICALITY.` → `AN EMPEROR'S NOTE.`

segments.voice: In Meditations six, twenty-one, Marcus says that if anyone can show him he isn't thinking or acting rightly, he'll gladly change. Not grudgingly. Gladly. His reason, in George Long's translation: "I seek the truth, by which no man was ever injured." The one harmed is the person who stays in their error. Being corrected feels like a loss; Marcus flips it. The correction is the gift. Staying wrong is the injury. And this is an emperor writing, and an emperor is easy to agree with. In book one he thanks his teacher Rusticus for showing him that his character needed correcting and discipline, and he praises his adoptive father, Antoninus, for listening to anyone with something useful for the common good. Read together, these lines suggest a man trying to make himself someone it was safe to correct. But the offer has a condition: show me. He isn't promising to change his mind for whoever is loudest, or whoever spoke last. He's asking for a reason. That's a high bar for others, and a higher one for yourself, because when you are shown, you really do move. Not later, not after saving face. Changing your own mind, out loud, takes a small courage, and an ordinary day offers the chance more than once.
screen: `SHOW ME, AND I'LL GLADLY CHANGE.` · `TRUTH NEVER INJURED ANYONE.` · `SAFE TO CORRECT AN EMPEROR.` · `THE CONDITION: SHOW ME.` · then, large: `SHOW ME.`

segments.voice: Hold one opinion you're firm about, a person, a plan, a habit, and ask honestly what someone would need to show you to change it. Picture them showing it, and notice any flinch or urge to defend. Then imagine saying, gladly, you're right, and rest with how that sentence sits.
Rusticus, the teacher Marcus thanks for showing him his character needed correction, behind the emperor's offer: show me I'm wrong, and I'll gladly change. Today's word.
Your line: show me. Being corrected is the gift; staying wrong is the injury. Day five hundred seventy-nine, done.

howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often hold to 6.21 as a habit of inviting correction: asking colleagues or friends to point out where they're wrong, and saying plainly when they've been shown.
